title: Fixed-player number-on-forehead disjointness exponent
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge2\), determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the communication exponent \[x_{\mathrm{NOF}}(k)=\inf\{a\ge0:R(n,k)=O_k(n^a)\text{ as }n\to\infty\}.\] Here \(R(n,k)\) is the minimum worst-case public-coin randomized communication for deciding whether \(k\) subsets of \([n]\) have empty common intersection, with error at most \(1/3\); player \(i\) sees every set except the \(i\)-th. The full interactive broadcast model and asymptotic quantifiers are below.
why: Each player knows almost the entire input, which makes communication lower bounds much harder than in the ordinary split-input model. Set disjointness gives a concrete way to measure how this overlap and additional players change the power of randomized interaction. A full answer would clarify a basic limitation used in several connections between communication, circuits and proofs.
status_note: Known results determine the constant-factor answer when the number of players is at least logarithmic in the universe size, and give strong lower bounds in smaller-player regimes. The bounded source review found no matching characterization over the full parameter domain. The consolidated historical three-player lower-bound threshold is already resolved, and the 2026 one-way deterministic result does not settle the active randomized target.

sentences: In number-on-forehead communication, each player sees every input set except its own.
The task is to decide whether all sets have empty common intersection.
The card asks for the polynomial exponent of randomized communication in the universe size.
Each fixed number of players has its own exponent, to absolute accuracy 0.01.
Local computation is free and arbitrary interactive public broadcasts are allowed.

context_blocks.text: The overlapping views are essential: with two players this recovers the usual two-party problem, while additional players see different nearly complete views. A lower bound for private-input message passing cannot simply be substituted.

For every fixed \(k\ge3\), the directional-derivative theorem yields a randomized lower bound of order \(\sqrt n\). Its explicit dependence is \(\Omega(\sqrt n/(2^k k))\). This does not match the general linear upper bound at a fixed small player count.

For \(n\ge2\) and \(k\ge\max\{2,\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\}\), the 2020 result determines the communication cost as \(\Theta(1+\log_2 n/\log_2(1+k/\log_2 n))\), uniformly in that regime. The selected numerical exponent instead concerns each fixed player count as the universe size tends to infinity.

The consolidated Jukna question only asks for a three-party deterministic lower bound growing faster than \((\log n)^3\). The known randomized polynomial lower bound already implies that historical threshold. It is not a second unresolved target here.

The numerical target keeps each fixed player count but no longer asks for a sharp bound uniform when the number of players grows with the universe. It determines polynomial exponents only; logarithmic factors and player-dependent multiplicative constants are outside its acceptance criterion.

Each fixed player count has its own exponent and may use its own multiplicative constants. The answer must approximate every such exponent within \(1/100\), but no uniform control of these constants as the number of players grows is requested.

source_consolidations.note: A super-log-cubed lower bound for three-party number-on-forehead disjointness is one specific milestone within the full communication-complexity problem. That threshold is preserved as context rather than a second independent target.

definitions:
The universe \([n]\) is \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Each \(S_j\) is represented by its characteristic vector \(x^{(j)}\in\{0,1\}^n\), where \(x^{(j)}_t=1\) means \(t\in S_j\). There is no restriction on set sizes, intersections, repeated sets, or the number of players relative to \(n\). In particular, \(k\) can exceed \(n\). The predicate asks for an empty intersection of all sets, not pairwise disjointness. Equivalently, the complementary predicate asks whether some row of the \(n\)-by-\(k\) incidence matrix is all ones; complementing the common output leaves the communication complexity unchanged.

All players know \(n,k\), their labels and the protocol. Player \(i\)'s initial view is the ordered tuple \((x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(i-1)},x^{(i+1)},\ldots,x^{(k)})\). No player initially sees its missing column. This is the number-on-forehead model; it is different from giving player \(i\) only \(S_i\).

A deterministic protocol is a finite binary tree. An internal node specifies which player broadcasts the next bit. That bit can be any function of that player's visible input and the preceding public transcript. The bit is written once on a blackboard and is seen by all players; broadcasting one bit costs one bit, not \(k\) bits. Each leaf specifies a common output bit. The speaker and the decision to stop are determined by the public node, so they cannot transmit an uncharged input-dependent signal. The players may speak in any order prescribed by the tree and may return arbitrarily often; neither the number of rounds nor the number of messages is separately bounded.

A public-coin randomized protocol is a distribution over deterministic protocols, selected using shared randomness independent of the inputs. Its cost is the maximum depth of any tree in the support. This bound is over all inputs and all random outcomes, not an expectation. For every full input tuple, the probability that the common output equals \(\operatorname{DISJ}_{n,k}\) must be at least \(2/3\). No private communication, pre-shared secret or quantum resource is provided.

Local computation, storage and the complexity of the protocol description are free. Protocols may be chosen independently for each pair \((n,k)\); there is no uniform algorithm for generating them or local running-time requirement. The model therefore asks about communication alone.

Define \(R(n,k)\) to be the least integer \(d\ge0\) for which such a randomized protocol of cost at most \(d\) exists. This set of costs is nonempty: one player can transmit a missing column to another, who can broadcast the answer, using at most \(n+1\) bits. Both output values occur for every allowed \((n,k)\), so a zero-communication output independent of the input cannot attain error \(1/3\) on all inputs. Thus \(1\le R(n,k)\le n+1\).

For each fixed integer \(k\ge2\), define \[x_{\mathrm{NOF}}(k)=\inf\{a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}:\exists C>0\ \exists n_0\ge1\ \forall n\ge n_0,\ R(n,k)\le Cn^a\}.\] The constant and threshold may depend on \(k\) and \(a\). The elementary bounds above ensure \(0\le x_{\mathrm{NOF}}(k)\le1\). The infimum need not be attained. The target does not require matching logarithmic factors, a uniform constant as \(k\) grows with \(n\), or a single protocol generator. Lower bounds must apply to all permitted randomized interactive protocols.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguously specified real answer \(a(k)\) for every integer \(k\ge2\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of absolute error at most \(1/100\) in the defined exponent. A certified enclosing interval of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies via its midpoint. Both sides of the interval must be justified. An exact value also qualifies. The infimum need not be attained, and no ordinary logarithmic growth limit is assumed. Matching logarithmic factors, leading constants and an algorithm attaining the endpoint exponent are not required. A one-sided improvement alone qualifies only if the resulting certified interval is sufficiently narrow.
